B-trees vs hash indexes

A database index is a separate structure that lets the engine find rows without scanning the whole table. The two most common kinds are B-tree indexes and hash indexes, and they are good at different things.

A hash index maps each key through a hash function to a bucket. Lookups for an exact key are very fast, close to constant time, but the hashing destroys ordering, so a hash index cannot answer range queries such as "all orders between March and May".

A B-tree keeps keys sorted in a balanced tree of pages. Equality lookups take a logarithmic number of page reads, and because the keys are ordered the same index serves range scans, prefix matches and ORDER BY without an extra sort.

In practice, choose a hash index only when every query on the column is an exact-match lookup and the workload is dominated by such lookups. Otherwise the B-tree is the safer default, which is why most databases create B-trees unless you ask for something else.
